newsitem.title: ITALY: Berlusconi furious as Italian budget moves forward.
newsitem.headline: Berlusconi furious as Italian budget moves forward.

text.p: Former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi said on Wednesday that the government was trampling democracy underfoot as it accelerated its controversial 1997 budget through parliament.
Berlusconi's opposition centre-right Freedom Alliance walked out of the parliamentary budget debate earlier this week in protest at the package.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi, taking advantage of the rare calm which has fallen over the lower house since the boycott, has hastened the reading of the bill and attached disputed decrees onto the budget package to speed their passage into law.

The cabinet decrees, which are opposed by the Freedom Alliance and set to expire, are not directly related to the 1997 budget but will now be able to slide onto the statute books on the tail of the financial package.
"We're at red alert," a furious Berlusconi told reporters. "The country and its democracy are in serious danger."

Under a recent court ruling, the government was barred from continuing the traditional practice of re-issuing expiring decrees. Instead the draft bills have to be converted into law by parliament within 60 days or else dropped.
With nearly 20 decrees about to fall due, Prodi has had to resort to do-or-die confidence motions to ram the bills past opposition filibustering.

On Wednesday his government called three confidence votes in the Senate (upper house) to push into law three decrees, including one covering a rescue plan for Italy's largest southern bank, Banco di Napoli.
To keep confidence votes to a minimum, the government late last night hooked six decrees onto the budget.
"There is no precedent for this kind of behaviour and it shows the level of arrogance...within the majority," the leader of the hardright National Alliance, Gianfranco Fini said.
The under-secretary for parliamentary relations, Giorgio Bogi, told reporters the government had tried to reach an agreement with the opposition but had failed.
"The government did not want to attach (the decrees) to the budget but had no other option," he added.

Voting on the budget continued apace in the lower house, with the centre-left coalition, supported by the hard-line Communist Refoundation, approving a controversial overhaul of Italy's complex fiscal system -- a revision which lies at the heart of Berlusconi's budget boycott.

The main bulk of the budget, which is designed to slash 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) off next year's deficit, is scheduled to be approved by the end of Thursday -- faster than most commentators had thought possible a week ago.
After this, the package is due to go to the Senate for ratification.

Prodi has said the budget is vital if Italy is to become a founder member of the planned single European currency. He has also said that as soon as the bill has been approved by the lower house, he will seek to put the lira back into the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM).

Many analysts believe it will re-enter the currency grid by the end of the month. Italy's economic prospects helped the financial markets shrug off the tense political climate, with bond futures hitting an all time high in early trade.
